# Oncology

The Oncology department will work with your primary care veterinarian to provide the comprehensive care your pet needs. Our oncologists have extensive training in a wide range of medical oncology services and treatments, and the most advanced equipment at his disposal. They specialize in the most current methods to diagnose and treat cancer while striving to preserve an excellent quality of life for the patient.

Our Oncology team provides comprehensive medical oncology services, incorporating chemotherapy and immunotherapy protocols. We work collaboratively with other department specialists in surgery, diagnostic imaging, interventional radiology and physical therapy & rehabilitation to provide our patients with a thoughtfully tailored approach to diagnosis and treatment.

### Some common signs of cancer in pets include:

  * Abnormal swellings that persist or continue to grow

  * Non-healing sores

  * Weight loss despite adequate food intake

### Common cancers diagnosed in dogs and cats include:

  * Lymphoma

    * Feline Lymphoma

    * Canine Lymphoma

  * Osteosarcoma

  * Mast cell tumor

  * Mammary tumors

  * Bladder tumors

  * Melanoma

  * Hemangiosarcoma

  * Soft tissue sarcomas

### Diagnostics

The diagnostic process involves tests to identify the type of cancer, as well as “staging” to determine whether the cancer has spread to other areas of the body. Some of the diagnostic techniques that we use in the process may include:

  * Complete Staging

  * Fine Needle Aspirates & Cytology

  * Solid Biopsy & Histopathology

  * Blood Chemistry Evaluations

  * Immunocytochemistry

  * Immunophenotyping

  * Computed Tomography (CT Scan)

  * Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)

  * Radiography (X-Rays)

  * Ultrasound

### Treatment Options

  * Chemotherapy and Targeted therapies

  * Immunotherapy

  * Palliative Care & Pain Management

  * Surgical Oncology

# Cancer center offers the latest in diagnostic, treatment services

### From offering specialty care to plans for a significant expansion in the field of translational research, learn about how the UC Davis Comparative Cancer Center aims to shape the future of cancer care.

April 9, 2026

By By Don Vaughan

Katja Guevara, RVT, and Gabby Hovey, RVT, prepare a dog for radiation therapy on the linear accelerator. PHOTO COURTESY MICHAEL BANNASCH, UC DAVIS WEILL SCHOOL OF VETERINARY MEDICINE

In late 2023, Klydee, an 11-year-old female terrier mix owned by Jeanne Maeda and Lori Tsuhako of Honolulu, Hawaii, developed a bulging right eye and worsening vision that ultimately led to blindness. Klydee was evaluated by a surgical oncologist in Honolulu, who identified a mass at the back of her right eye, arising from nervous tissue.

Klydee's tumor was initially removed, but tumor cells were left behind. Because radiation therapy is not available in Hawaii, the dog was subsequently referred for radiation therapy at the UC Davis Weill School of Veterinary Medicine's Comparative Cancer Center.

We understand that your pet is a part of your family, and we strive to treat you and your pet with the utmost empathy and respect for your relationship and bond.

Our team works to ensure that patients receive the best care and follow-up treatment possible by communicating with your referring veterinarian.

The well-being and comfort of our patients and their families is the primary focus of our efforts. We treat our animal patients like family members.

#### DVM, MS, DACVIM-Oncology

# Kaitlin Esson

Dr. Esson earned her Bachelor of Science with honors from American University before completing a Master’s degree in microbiology and biogeochemistry at the Georgia Institute of Technology. She went on to receive her Doctor of Veterinary Medicine from Oregon State University, where she discovered her passion for oncology during her third year of veterinary school.

After graduation, Dr. Esson completed a rotating internship at the University of Illinois and then went on to an oncology residency at NC State University. She has a special interest in hospice care and is especially passionate about supporting feline oncology patients and their families.

When she’s not caring for her patients, Dr. Esson enjoys practicing Bikram yoga, hiking on local trails, and spending time with her two rescue cats Biscuit and Grimm.

## What is a Board Certified Surgeon

And Why Would I Need One?

Advances in animal health care have led to a wider variety of treatment options, including highly specialized surgical procedures. Board-certified surgeons spend at least four years after achieving their veterinary medical degree focusing strictly on surgery.

> This concentrated training in surgery allows the ACVS Veterinary Surgeon to keep current with frequent advances in veterinary medicine. Board-certified surgeons are skilled in advanced orthopedic, abdominal, thoracic, neurologic, oncologic, and reconstructive surgeries. If your pet requires a surgical procedure, ask your veterinarian if consultation with a specialist is indicated. General procedures, including spays, neuters, and many broken bones, may be less likely to require someone who is board-certified.

##### Rachel Venable, DVM, MS, DACVIM (Oncology)

Image

Dr. Venable is a medical oncologist who has always been surrounded by animals growing up on a farm in the Midwest. She obtained her veterinary degree from the University of Missouri and graduated cum laude. After veterinary school, Dr. Venable pursued further training as a small animal intern at the University of Georgia. She then completed her 3-year medical oncology residency at the world-renowned Colorado State Flint Animal Cancer Center. During her residency, she achieved a master’s degree and studied new cancer therapies and clinical trials. She continues to seek out clinical trials and cutting-edge therapies for her patients. Dr. Venable has authored numerous publications and has been a speaker on local and national levels. She is the founder of Pet Cancer Care Consulting, an innovative teleconsulting service which consults with the family vet and pet owner together to give personalized responses and needed information to make an informed decision on treatments.

COMMITTEE ON CONSUMER PROTECTION & COMMERCE  
Rep. Aaron Ling Johanson, Chair  
Rep. Lisa Kitagawa, Vice Chair  

DATE: Wednesday, March 30, 2022  
TIME: 2:00 P.M.  
PLACE: VIA VIDEOCONFERENCE  
Conference Room 329  
State Capitol  
415 South Beretania Street  

Dear Representative Johanson, Representative Kitagawa and members of the committee,

SB2798 SD1 HD1 is a vitally important bill for Hawaii's animals, pet owners and veterinarians and I urge you to give it your full support.

Qualified out-of-state veterinarians had been allowed to practice in Hawaii until recently. A number of stakeholders, from the veterinary community to animal welfare groups, worked together to draft this bill and restore that important lifeline.

There is a nationwide shortage of veterinarians and there are open positions across our state in both private clinics and animal shelters, putting stress on local veterinarians.

Both private clinics and animal welfare nonprofits rely on qualified out-of-state veterinarians for relief support and the provision of expertise that is rare or completely unavailable in the state, such as dermatology, oncology, and forensic veterinary medicine.

Please pass SB2798 SD1 HD1 and allow veterinarians licensed in good standing in other states or Canada to work in Hawaii at the invitation of our local veterinarians.

Mahalo for your consideration.

Sincerely,  
Natalie Spencer  
Honolulu, HI 96825
